subChunks.title: String Methods & Immutability
subChunks.hookHtml: Every spell in the Arcane Academy is recorded on a scroll — precise, immutable, and searchable. In Java, text is stored in String objects. Learning to manipulate them fluently is one of the most useful skills in the entire language.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Strings are Immutable

Once a String is created, its characters cannot be changed. Every method that 'modifies' a String actually returns a new String:

String s = "hello";
String upper = s.toUpperCase();  // "HELLO" — s is still "hello"
System.out.println(s);     // hello
System.out.println(upper); // HELLO

Essential String Methods

String spell = "Fireball";

spell.length()          // 8 — number of characters
spell.charAt(0)         // 'F' — character at index 0
spell.toUpperCase()     // "FIREBALL"
spell.toLowerCase()     // "fireball"
spell.contains("ball")  // true
spell.startsWith("Fire")// true
spell.endsWith("ball")  // true
spell.indexOf("ball")   // 4 — index of first occurrence
spell.substring(4)      // "ball" — from index 4 to end
spell.substring(0, 4)   // "Fire" — from 0, up to (not including) 4
spell.replace('l','r')  // "Firebar" — replaces all 'l'
spell.trim()            // removes leading and trailing whitespace
spell.isEmpty()         // false — returns true only if length == 0
spell.isBlank()         // false — returns true if empty or only whitespace (Java 11+)

String Comparison

Never compare Strings with ==. That compares object references (memory addresses), not content. Use .equals():

String a = new String("hello");
String b = new String("hello");
// a == b   →  false (different objects)
// a.equals(b) → true (same content)

For case-insensitive comparison: a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)

String Concatenation

Use + to join strings. Java auto-converts other types:

int mana = 42;
String msg = "Mana: " + mana;  // "Mana: 42"

split()

String csv = "fire,ice,earth";
String[] elements = csv.split(",");  // ["fire", "ice", "earth"]
System.out.println(elements[1]);     // ice

storyBeats.text: In the Academy's inscription chamber, scrolls glow softly on every shelf. A precision-focused wizard is examining one under a magnifying glass, muttering about indexing.

storyBeats.speaker: Scribe Nara
storyBeats.text: A String is a sequence of characters. Once inscribed, a scroll cannot be altered — in Java we say Strings are immutable. Every method that appears to change a String actually produces a new one. The original scroll remains untouched.

storyBeats.speaker: Strings are immutable
Scribe Nara
storyBeats.text: Characters in a String are indexed exactly like array elements — from zero. The method charAt(index) retrieves a single character. substring(start, end) extracts a range: it includes the start index but excludes the end. Forgetting the exclusive end is a frequent source of bugs.

storyBeats.speaker: charAt and substring
storyBeats.text:
String rune = "Shadowstep";
System.out.println(rune.charAt(0));      // S
System.out.println(rune.substring(6));   // step
System.out.println(rune.substring(0,6)); // Shadow

storyBeats.speaker: Scribe Nara
storyBeats.text: Critical rule: never compare Strings with ==. That tests whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory — not whether the content is the same. == gives correct results by accident sometimes (due to string interning) but will betray you. Always use .equals().

storyBeats.speaker: String comparison

learningObjectives: Explain String immutability and why String methods return new values instead of modifying in place
Use length(), charAt(), substring(), contains(), indexOf(), replace(), trim(), split()
Compare String content correctly using .equals() and .equalsIgnoreCase()
Concatenate Strings and other types using the + operator
commonMistakes: Using == to compare String content — always use .equals()
Forgetting that substring(start, end) excludes the end index
Not storing the result of a String method — the original String is never changed
Calling methods on a null String — results in NullPointerException

Can explain why a == b can be false even when both Strings contain identical characters

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain String immutability to a complete beginner. Why can't you change a String in place? What actually happens when you call toUpperCase()? Use an analogy that makes the concept intuitive.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A spell catalogue entry arrives as a raw String. Process it:

  1. Given String entry = " Thunderclap:80:lightning ", trim whitespace and store in cleaned
  2. Print the length of cleaned
  3. Split by ":" into an array called parts. Print the spell name (index 0) in upper case.
  4. Print the power value at index 1
  5. Print whether the entry contains the word "lightning"
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From scratch. Given String scroll = "Arcane Missile — tier:SENIOR — damage:150":

  • Print the character at index 0
  • Print the substring from index 0 to 14 (the spell name)
  • Print the scroll in lower case
  • Print the index of the first '-' character

  • Replace all occurrences of ':' with '=' and print the result

questions.questionHtml: Which method should you use to compare two String values for equal content?
questions.explanationHtml: .equals() compares the character content of two Strings. == compares object references (memory addresses), which can give unexpected false results even for identical strings. Use .equalsIgnoreCase() when case should be ignored.
substring(5, 9) returns characters at indices 5, 6, 7, 8 (the end index is exclusive): 'c','a','s','t' → "cast".
Strings are immutable. toUpperCase() returns a new String. The original s remains unchanged. To use the upper-case version, assign it: String upper = s.toUpperCase();
Splitting by "," gives 4 parts: fire, water, earth, air. parts.length = 4. parts[2] = "earth".

questions.questionHtml: A developer runs this code expecting it to check whether user input equals "admin". What is wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: == compares object references, not content — even if input contains "admin" it may be a different String object; use input.equals("admin") instead
questions.explanationHtml: String literals may be interned (making == work accidentally), but user input or strings from external sources are rarely the same object. The safe and correct approach is always .equals(). Also consider null safety: "admin".equals(input) avoids NPE if input is null.

subChunks.title: String Building & Formatting
subChunks.hookHtml: When a scribe must copy the same scroll template fifty times, filling in different names and values each time, they don't hand-copy every letter. They use a template with blanks. In Java, that is StringBuilder and String.format().
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why Not Just Use +?

The + operator creates a new String object every time. In a loop, this generates many temporary objects:

// Inefficient: creates ~10 String objects
String result = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    result += i;  // new String each iteration
}

StringBuilder

StringBuilder maintains a mutable character buffer. Append to it in a loop, then convert to String once:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    sb.append(i).append(", ");
}
String result = sb.toString();  // "0, 1, 2, 3, 4, "

Key methods: append(), insert(index, str), delete(start, end), reverse(), length(), toString(). append() returns this, enabling method chaining.

String.format()

Templates with placeholders for cleaner, readable string construction:

String name = "Lyria";
int level = 7;
double power = 93.5;
String report = String.format("Mage %s (Level %d) — Power: %.1f", name, level, power);
// "Mage Lyria (Level 7) — Power: 93.5"

Common format specifiers:

  • %s — String
  • %d — integer
  • %f — float/double (default 6 decimal places)
  • %.2f — float with 2 decimal places
  • %n — platform-appropriate newline

Formatted Strings with printf

System.out.printf() prints directly with the same format specifiers, without creating an intermediate String.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's printing press is clattering away in the basement. An apprentice is building spell labels by stitching together short strings in a loop — and the press has slowed to a crawl. The foreman arrives.

storyBeats.speaker: Press Foreman Dax
storyBeats.text: Every + inside a loop creates a new String object and discards the old one. Your loop is littering the memory with ghost Strings. Use a StringBuilder — one mutable buffer. You append to it, and when you're done, call toString() once.

storyBeats.speaker: StringBuilder in a loop
Press Foreman Dax
storyBeats.text: For label templates, use String.format(). Place %s for a String placeholder, %d for an integer, %.2f for a double with two decimal places. Cleaner and more readable than concatenation chains.

storyBeats.speaker: String.format for spell labels

learningObjectives: Explain why concatenating strings in a loop with + is inefficient
Use StringBuilder to build a string iteratively with append(), then toString()
Format output using String.format() with %s, %d, and %f specifiers
Choose between +, StringBuilder, and String.format() based on context
commonMistakes: Using StringBuilder for simple two-string concatenations — the + operator is fine and readable for a small fixed number of joins
Forgetting to call toString() after building with StringBuilder
Using %f when you want %s — causes runtime IllegalFormatException
assessmentCriteria: Can build a comma-separated list from an array using StringBuilder without a trailing separator
Can format a report line with fixed column widths using String.format()
Can explain when to use StringBuilder vs simple + concatenation
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Why is using + to concatenate strings inside a loop inefficient, and how does StringBuilder solve the problem? Explain as if teaching a fellow student who just learned about strings.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a spell roster string from an array:

  1. Given String[] spells = {"Fireball", "Frostbolt", "Thunderwave", "Shadowstep"}, use a StringBuilder to build a comma-separated list: "Fireball, Frostbolt, Thunderwave, Shadowstep" (no trailing comma)
  2. Then use String.format() to print: "Roster (4 spells): Fireball, Frostbolt, Thunderwave, Shadowstep"

guidedPracticeTests.label: Formatted output correct
guidedPracticeTests.expected: Roster (4 spells): Fireball, Frostbolt, Thunderwave, Shadowstep

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From scratch. Given double[] powers = {72.5, 88.0, 45.333, 99.1}:

  • Use StringBuilder to build a string listing each power formatted to 1 decimal place, separated by " / ". No trailing separator.
  • Print the total using String.format(): "Total power: 304.9" (1 decimal place)

questions.questionHtml: Which format specifier represents a double with exactly 2 decimal places in String.format()?
questions.explanationHtml: %.2f formats a floating-point number with 2 decimal places. %d is for integers, %s is for strings, and %2d is an integer with minimum width 2.
Each append() call adds to the buffer in sequence. The final toString() produces "Spell:42XP".
